No, This disproportionately affects poorer people.

For example, if you make 1000 a month, you get 900 after taxes.

If you make 100k a month, you would pay 10k and have 90k after taxes.

Now, everyone has a baseline that is needed. Food and shelter, etc. The costs don't vary much per person (overall, in my area eating crappy for a month is 200 and eating well is 500 a month).

Basically, you're asking about fair inputs and fair outputs. This is a "fair input". What happens is that it brings around unfair outputs. Now, this isn't completely unwanted. BUT, in today end game capitalism we have, you would essentially create a worse situation than we have now where taxes come from the poorest of the people.

One of the alternatives is a graduated flat tax (im not sure of the terminology). Everyone pays something, the lowest .5% and the highest pay 25%. Where at the age with technology, we can make it truly graduated, so that you don't get the tax brackets.

The concept that it costs a certain amount to survive is way too understated when the flat tax conversation comes up. When a poor family's car breaks down, which they do from time to time, that's 600 dollars off of their 900 after taxes, but 600 dollars off of 90k is basically nothing to the rich family. The consequences for the poor family are exponentially higher when financial obligations inevitably occur. It also makes it that much harder to become a skilled laborer when you either can't afford the education, or are working too many unskilled jobs to have the time to concentrate on any one of them to advance.

Somewhat fair, but a national sales tax would be fairer. If you buy a loaf of bread, you pay little tax. You buy a yacht, you pay a lot. Everyone pays something and no free rides. No exemptions, no loop holes, no IRS. Well much, much smaller IRS would be needed.
